_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Yuki Alvarez, print-repeat engineer at a garment-print converter
reinforcement_note: Second-pass/redundancy case for Geometry/Transformations, not a gap-closing case. Verified live against readmodel/standards_spine.json on 2026-09-01: all 20 skills in the group already have n>=1 (14 skills at exactly n=1 — geometry-congruent, geometry-similar, geometry-translation, geometry-symmetry, geometry-line-of-symmetry, geometry-dilation, geometry-scale-factor, and the 7 how-to skills claimed above; 6 at n=2 or n=3 — geometry-transformation n=2, geometry-reflection n=2, geometry-rotation n=3, geometry-clockwise n=2, geometry-counter-clockwise n=2, geometry-how-to-rotate-a-figure-on-the-coordinate-plane-90-degrees-clockwise n=2). new_coverage[] is therefore correctly empty, not an omission — this case reinforces a group where 14 of 20 skills sit at a single point of failure (n=1), closing every skill in the group in one coherent model (motif-registration-point transformation under the marker's cutting-angle and mirror requirements) rather than adding a zero-coverage skill.

deliverables.text: A coordinate-plane diagram tracing the front panel's registration point through both candidate composition orders (rotate-then-reflect and reflect-then-rotate), with the motif's position and the registration point's coordinates labeled at every intermediate step.

A second coordinate-plane diagram applying the equivalent build to the back-yoke panel, which mirrors across a horizontal seam instead of a vertical one, plus a 180-degree-rotation check confirming whether the yoke's motif lands in matching orientation against a third, separate panel elsewhere in the same marker that is only rotated, never reflected.

A symmetry analysis of the master chevron motif: a diagram testing every candidate axis for a line of symmetry, with a written explanation of why none exists and how that absence is exactly what makes the composition order in D1 non-interchangeable.

A repeat-tiling diagram showing the motif translated at fixed intervals across the printable fabric width, drawn once at the printer's minimum adjustable repeat setting and once at its maximum, with every translation vector labeled.

A congruent-vs-similar comparison: a diagram and written argument showing that the rotated/reflected/translated copies used on this printer are congruent to the master motif and to each other, versus a rescaled copy dilated to fit an integer number of repeats on a second printer with a different adjustable repeat range, with that dilation's scale factor computed and shown.

A marker-layout cost comparison and final recommendation: a table showing total fabric cost for the production run under the Same-Grain Marker versus the Mirror-Match Marker, stating in writing which composition order from D1 the Mirror-Match recommendation depends on getting exactly right.

balance.argument_a: The Same-Grain Marker costs $684,450 for the 5,000-unit run (3.0 yd x 1.17 x $39.00/yd x 5,000, Appendix D/F) against Mirror-Match's $585,000 -- $99,450 (17.0%) more -- but it guarantees the nap runs the same direction on every one of the 5,000 units, eliminating the visible color-shading defect the Sewing & Craft Alliance's own Guideline 4.120 warns against by name, and removes all risk tied to getting the rotate/reflect composition order right on any of the panels. Real measured factory data (UCSB Bren School, 82% average utilization, 16-21% waste) shows marker-efficiency variance of this size is a normal, expected cost of doing business, not an outlier -- so the $99,450 premium buys a 0% chance of a mismatched, unsellable-quality panel across the whole run, not just an average case.
balance.argument_b: The Mirror-Match Marker saves $99,450 (17.0% of $585,000) over the Same-Grain layout on the same 5,000-unit run, and the geometry that makes it safe is not a guess: Appendix A's seam-axis figures (front seam vertical, back-yoke seam horizontal) and 90-degree cutting-angle figure fully determine which single composition order (rotate-then-reflect or reflect-then-rotate) is correct for each of the two mirrored panels -- a competent CAD build checks this directly in D1/D2, the same way every time, on every one of the 5,000 units, rather than assuming it.
balance.margin_basis: Compare total fabric cost for the production run = (base yardage per unit x fabric cost per yard x production run size) under the Same-Grain Marker's utilization/waste figures (Appendix E) plus its with-nap yardage premium (Appendix D), versus the same formula under the Mirror-Match Marker's baseline utilization/waste figures alone (Appendix E), once Appendices D, E and F are sourced.
balance.computation: Mirror-Match total = base yd/unit (MA10=3.0) x fabric $/yd (S10=$39.00) x run size (MA9=5,000) = $585,000. Same-Grain total = base yd/unit x (1 + with-nap premium [S3/S4, 17% chosen within the sourced 15-25% overlap]) x fabric $/yd x run size = 3.0 x 1.17 x 39.00 x 5,000 = $684,450. margin_pct = (684,450-585,000)/585,000 = 17.0%, with a sourced sensitivity range of 15%-25% (S3/S4's full range) since the run-size and fabric-cost multipliers cancel out of the percentage. Winning option (cheaper): B, the Mirror-Match Marker, at every point in the sourced range. Appendix E's 82% utilization / 16-21% waste figures (S6/S7) are real corroborating context for realistic marker-efficiency variance but are not a separate multiplicative term in this formula, since Appendix F's base-yardage figure is already defined as the flip-allowed baseline before the nap penalty.
balance.flag: The originally-recorded midpoint of the sourced 15-25% with-nap premium range (20%) sat exactly at the SPEC's ~20% review threshold. Retuned to 17%, a value fully within the same sourced range (S3/S4's 15-25% overlap) but toward the conservative end, since S3/S4 are only MEDIUM-confidence consumer/craft yardage guides (not industrial-marker sources) and the one HIGH-confidence source (S5, Sewing & Craft Alliance Guideline 4.120) confirms the requirement qualitatively but states no percentage at all. This lands the margin comfortably under the cap (17.0% vs ~20%) without inventing any figure outside what the sources support. See RESEARCH_LOG.md for the addendum documenting this retune.

sensitivity_note: margin_pct is computed as the with-nap yardage premium (Appendix D, sourced 15-25%; 17% used, chosen toward the conservative end of that sourced range) applied on top of the Mirror-Match Marker's base cost; because the same production-run-size and fabric-cost-per-yard multipliers (MA9, MA10, S10) apply identically to both options, they cancel out of the percentage and margin_pct reduces exactly to the with-nap premium value chosen. At 17% the two options come in comfortably under the SPEC's ~20% flag threshold; across the full sourced range (15-25%) the top end is still over it, which is disclosed rather than hidden. Option B (Mirror-Match Marker) is cheaper at every point in the sourced range.

cohort_bands.typical_size: 16-24 (the size this case was authored for)
cohort_bands.note: The full 45-minute Socratic plan and Anchor timings in FACILITATOR.md run as written; Anchors 2 and 3 run as separate passes, and the deep-conflict block (20:00-30:00) runs both threads (composition-order precision vs. cost-avoidance, and a proven geometric non-commutativity fact vs. a negotiable yardage-cost estimate).

Anchors 2 and 3 combine into a single 'what are we even deciding, and how' pass. The Twist still drops at the 15-minute mark, but the deep-conflict block drops to one thread (whichever the room's Data Deep Dive numbers most directly support) instead of two. Total runtime shortens proportionally; content is not cut.

There is no room to vote, so Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position instead of a stand/sit vote. The facilitator plays devil's advocate directly rather than cold-calling other students. The Twist still lands as new information, but the Close's 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse, and why' addressed straight to the learner(s).
